A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same SMC framework, with matching title, authors, core methods and experiments. Text, equations, tables, figures and complete appendices support reliable comparison, including matching relocated and renumbered material.

before.justification: v3 reports original experiments on synthetic distributions, MNIST, toxic text generation, DNA design and image generation, including quantitative results and appendix analyses.

after.justification: v4 retains these original empirical results and adds baseline comparisons, an ESS diagnostic and computational-cost measurements.

M1.justification: The core SMC algorithms, amortised proposal and training objective remain unchanged. Appendix C.2 adds an optional REINFORCE estimator for first-order proposals with nondifferentiable rewards, whereas v3's first-order route assumed differentiable rewards. Its expanded Gumbel-Softmax explanation documents an existing procedure; the new alternative is not experimentally evaluated.

E1.justification: Both versions retain MoG, binary MNIST, toxic text generation, regulatory DNA design, ImageNet256 and the same text-to-image prompt collections and rewards. New comparisons and diagnostics reuse this coverage; no additional dataset, task or input-environment scenario is evaluated.

E2.justification: v4 substantially expands external comparisons: Table 4 adds SVDD at N=2,4,8,16 for toxic text generation, and Table 5 adds SVDD at N=8,16 and SGDD at beta=30,50 for DNA design. The earlier BoN, CG, CFG, DRAKES and proposal/SMC comparators remain. SVDD's citation in v3 did not constitute an evaluated comparison.

E3.justification: Appendix D.1.2 changes the stated Meissonic training budget from 250 to 300 epochs, without establishing that retained results were rerun. The new MNIST diagnostic uses 16 particles without resampling, and the timing study measures generation of one image from one prompt across particle counts. The added SGDD comparison uses uniform noising, unlike the masked-diffusion comparators.

E4.justification: Beyond the retained schedule, Monte Carlo sample-count and sampling-scheme analyses, v4 adds a controlled investigation of proposal-dependent ESS and reward trajectories without resampling, accompanied by generated MNIST samples (Figures 12–13). Appendix D.2.6 also examines training and inference costs. These additions directly assess weight degeneracy and computational tradeoffs previously unmeasured.

E5.justification: v4 specifies 30 independent runs for the new ESS/reward experiment and displays shaded bands in Figure 12, although their statistical meaning is not defined. Existing three-seed DNA reporting and 30-run MNIST schedule ablations are unchanged. The additional DNA baseline rows retain the existing mean-and-standard-deviation reporting practice.

E6.justification: Matched original scores and plots are retained, but substantial new results are added. Table 4 reports SVDD toxicity/holdout toxicity of 97.5%/91.0% at N=16. Table 5 adds SGDD and SVDD outcomes under their stated settings. Figures 12–13 add ESS and sample-quality findings; Table 6 reports N=16 inference times of 48.47 seconds for BoN, 80.61 for SMCbase/amot and 181.26 for SMCgrad. These are added comparisons, not improvements over v3's scores.

T1.justification: Proposition 1 explicitly adds the detailed-balance condition already used in v3's appendix proof, and Appendix C.2 derives the score-function gradient alternative. The central optimal-proposal and log-variance proofs remain unchanged. The new SMC recap also introduces mathematical slips: its importance-sampling estimator omits the 1/N factor, and its weight-update indices do not match the propagation step.

C1.justification: The abstract, introduction's contribution statements and conclusion retain the same claims: tractable SMC control, two approximately optimal proposals, log-variance training and effective inference-time scaling across domains. The added evidence does not redefine these main contributions.

C2.justification: New discussion attributes Propgrad's poorer ESS and samples to proposal bias and reward hacking. The DNA discussion interprets SGDD's weak correlations as mode collapse and SVDD's lower ATAC accuracy as reward hacking, while acknowledging SGDD's different noising process. The cost discussion explains overhead through repeated reward evaluations and gradient computation. These are additional interpretations, not established causal findings.

D1.justification: v4 adds a code-repository link, details the gradient path through denoising, Gumbel-Softmax sampling and reward evaluation, and reports approximately 300 GPU hours of Meissonic training plus inference timings. It also revises the documented epoch count. Most existing hardware, optimiser, batch-size and LoRA information remains unchanged; repository contents cannot be verified from the PDFs.

R1.justification: Section 5 expands coverage of embedding-space guidance, reward-free guidance, tree-search alignment and additional diffusion-SMC work. Sections 3.2 and B.2 add connections to annealed flow transport and Radon–Nikodym formulations. These broaden the existing discussion while preserving the proposal-centred distinction from prior fixed-proposal approaches.

P1.justification: v4 adds an SMC recap, an expanded gradient explanation, supplementary discussion and acknowledgements, and changes the preprint header to conference-publication text. Most main-text prose and the overall section sequence remain intact; there is no extensive narrative rewrite.

P2.justification: v4 adds ESS and sample figures, expands Tables 4–5 and introduces timing Table 6. Figure 14 redisplays the existing training reward curves against GPU hours. Original qualitative galleries are retained and renumbered from Figures 12–16 to 15–19. Layout changes are local reflow and additions rather than a general redesign.

improvement.justification: The added baselines, ESS diagnostic, computational costs and implementation explanations improve empirical scrutiny and practical assessability. These benefits outweigh localized weaknesses: the new SMC recap contains normalization and indexing errors, and some new reward-hacking and mode-collapse interpretations exceed what the proxy metrics establish. With the central method, claims and original results retained, the net improvement is useful but limited.
